title: EU–Kenya Youth Sounding Board 2026–2028: Applications Open for 15 Young Kenyan Leaders
summary: The European Union Delegation to Kenya has opened applications for the second cohort of the EU Youth Sounding Board, offering 15 young Kenyan leaders an opportunity to contribute their perspectives to the EU–Kenya partnership. The Youth Sounding Board brings together young people from different counties, communities, socioeconomic backgrounds and areas of expertise. Selected members will advise the European Union Delegation to Kenya on youth participation and empowerment while contributing to structured dialogue among young people, civil society organisations and the European Union. The Board is looking for collaborative, community-minded young leaders who are already engaged in youth organisations, civil society organisations, community-based organisations, networks, movements or other collective initiatives. Applications must be submitted by 31 August 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Nairobi time. The opportunity is voluntary, but reasonable expenses connected with participation will be covered by the META project. EU–Kenya Youth Sounding Board at a Glance Program detail Information Opportunity Second cohort of the EU–Kenya Youth Sounding Board Organiser Delegation of the European Union to Kenya Supporting initiative Meaningful Engagement–Transformative Action for Structured CSO Dialogue in Kenya Number of members 15 Eligible age 18–30 during the implementation period ending in March 2028 Eligible nationality Kenyan citizens Residency requirement Applicants must reside in Kenya Languages English and/or Swahili Participation format Regular meetings, consultations, policy dialogues and related activities Expected meeting frequency Approximately one meeting per month Nature of participation Voluntary Participation expenses Reasonable participation costs will be covered Application method Online Google application form Application deadline 31 August 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Nairobi time Anticipated onboarding 9–13 November 2026 Mandate period Through March 2028 The current call was published by the European Union Delegation to Kenya on 7 August 2026. What Is the EU–Kenya Youth Sounding Board? The EU Youth Sounding Board is a consultative mechanism that enables young people to contribute to the European Union’s policies, partnerships, programmes and engagement in Kenya. Its purpose is to ensure that decisions and programmes affecting young people are not designed without meaningful youth participation. Members provide advice, share community perspectives, identify emerging issues and help strengthen dialogue between young Kenyans, civil society and the European Union. The Board is intended to make the EU’s actions in Kenya: More participatory by involving young people in relevant discussions and consultation processes. More inclusive by incorporating perspectives from different counties, communities and social groups. More relevant by connecting policies and programmes with the actual priorities of young Kenyans. More responsive by identifying challenges experienced by youth, including marginalised and vulnerable groups. More effective by allowing young people and civil society organisations to contribute to program design and implementation. Members participate as individuals while drawing upon the experiences of the communities, organisations, networks and constituencies with which they are associated. Background to the EU Youth Sounding Board Initiative The European Union considers youth participation an important part of its international partnerships and external action. Under the EU Youth Action Plan 2022–2027, EU Delegations are encouraged to establish youth advisory mechanisms that can provide perspectives on country-specific priorities. The Kenya Youth Sounding Board draws inspiration from the EU Global Youth Sounding Board, first established in 2021 to provide young people with a structured role in advising the European Commission on international partnerships. The first EU–Kenya Youth Sounding Board was formally launched in 2024. It comprised 15 Kenyan leaders aged between 19 and 27 from different geographic and socioeconomic backgrounds. Its membership included representatives of pastoralist communities, refugees and persons with disabilities. The first cohort advised on program implementation and helped promote inclusive dialogue within the EU–Kenya partnership. Read about the first EU–Kenya cohort . The second cohort is intended to build on that foundation and deepen structured youth participation in EU-supported dialogue and cooperation. About the META Project The second Youth Sounding Board is being constituted through the Meaningful Engagement–Transformative Action for Structured CSO Dialogue in Kenya project, commonly referred to as META. META is a joint initiative of: The African Women’s Development and Communication Network, known as FEMNET. Stichting Women Engage for a Common Future International, known as WECF. The Delegation of the European Union to Kenya. The initiative seeks to strengthen the ability of Kenyan civil society organisations to contribute to accountability, good governance and inclusive development. It also supports institutional platforms through which civil society can participate in EU–Kenya cooperation. Its principal objectives include: Strengthening structured dialogue META promotes regular, inclusive and meaningful engagement among Kenyan civil society organisations, local authorities and the European Union. Building civil-society capacity The project supports the development of skills, knowledge and resources among civil society organisations, including youth organisations and women’s rights organisations. Improving coordination META encourages information sharing, joint planning and coordinated implementation among Kenyan civil society actors to improve the impact of EU–Kenya cooperation. Creating institutional platforms The project develops mechanisms through which civil society organisations and youth representatives can participate consistently in policy and development discussions. The Youth Sounding Board functions as an important youth-participation mechanism within this wider civil-society dialogue framework. How Will the Youth Sounding Board Work? The Board will comprise 15 members selected from across Kenya. Its composition is expected to reflect the country’s social, cultural, geographic and demographic diversity. Members will participate in approximately one meeting per month. The actual schedule will be determined by the work plan agreed between the Youth Sounding Board and the META consortium. Participation may also involve: Structured policy dialogues. Consultations with the EU Delegation. Engagement with civil society organisations. Meetings with youth networks and community organisations. Contributions to planning and program-design processes. Participation in public or stakeholder events. Engagement with the Inclusive Dialogue Platform. Input into annual EU–Kenya civil-society forums. Capacity-development and networking activities. Representation in relevant project-governance structures. Members will be expected to remain actively engaged throughout the implementation period ending in March 2028. Responsibilities of Youth Sounding Board Members Participate in structured dialogue Members will support regular consultations, policy debates and structured discussions involving the European Union, civil society actors and different Kenyan communities. These discussions may involve: Community-based organisations. Youth-led initiatives. Women’s organisations. Organisations representing persons with disabilities. Indigenous communities. Older persons and their representative groups. Civil society networks. Public authorities and other stakeholders. Identify youth policy priorities Members will help young people identify policy issues that directly affect them and bring those issues into the structured-dialogue process. This may involve gathering community perspectives, consulting youth constituencies and presenting evidence-based recommendations. Promote meaningful youth participation The Board will help ensure that youth participation is substantive rather than symbolic. Members are expected to support young people’s involvement in identifying priorities, discussing policy options and contributing to the implementation of relevant initiatives. Represent youth in project-governance structures Youth representatives may participate in the project’s Steering Committee and contribute to planning dialogue mechanisms and other major activities under the META initiative. Support the Inclusive Dialogue Platform Members will support youth-led and youth-based organisations participating in the Inclusive Dialogue Platform. This platform enables civil society organisations to convene periodic dialogue events leading to an annual high-level EU–Kenya civil-society forum. Contribute to priority areas of EU–Kenya cooperation The dialogue process is expected to address major areas of EU cooperation with Kenya, including: Green transition Digitalisation Youth participation Civil-society engagement Inclusive development Governance and accountability Communication and public visibility Social and economic opportunities for young people Advise the EU Delegation to Kenya Board members may provide youth perspectives on: EU programming in Kenya. Design of new actions and initiatives. Policy development. Communication campaigns. Visibility plans. Program implementation. Youth participation and empowerment. Implementation of the EU Youth Action Plan. Advise the META network Members will contribute advice and recommendations concerning the current and future implementation of META activities. Engage with communities and constituencies Members must maintain active engagement with the communities, organisations or networks they represent. They should bring community experiences into Board discussions and communicate relevant outcomes back to their constituencies where appropriate. Important Limitations and Confidentiality Requirements Youth Sounding Board members do not become official spokespersons for the European Union. Members must not: Claim to speak on behalf of the European Union Delegation to Kenya. Present themselves as authorised EU representatives. Speak officially for another country or region. Publish confidential Board discussions on social media. Share restricted documents or internal information. Use their membership in a manner inconsistent with the Board’s mandate. Confidentiality is intended to create an environment in which members and EU representatives can engage in open, constructive and trusted discussions. Before assuming their role, successful candidates will be required to sign: The Youth Sounding Board Terms of Reference. A Code of Conduct. A Declaration of Commitment. Is the Youth Sounding Board a Paid Position? Membership is voluntary. The official Terms of Reference do not advertise a salary, monthly stipend or employment contract. However, reasonable expenses associated with participation will be covered by the META project. The precise support available for each physical meeting or activity will be explained in a logistical note issued before the event. Applicants should therefore understand that this is a voluntary advisory and leadership commitment rather than paid employment. Expense coverage should not be interpreted as a salary or personal grant. Benefits of Joining the EU–Kenya Youth Sounding Board Practical policy-influencing experience Members will gain experience contributing to policy discussions and advising an international institution on youth participation, development programming and public engagement. Youth advocacy experience Participants will strengthen their ability to articulate youth priorities, develop recommendations and promote meaningful youth inclusion. National and international exposure Members may engage with youth networks and initiatives at local, national, regional and global levels. Representation of diverse youth voices Board members can bring attention to the experiences of communities that may be underrepresented in conventional policy discussions. Professional networking The Board offers opportunities to connect with: Other young Kenyan leaders. Civil society professionals. Youth organisations. Community advocates. Policy practitioners. Representatives of the European Union. Mentors and subject-matter specialists. Organisations working on governance and development. Leadership development Participation can strengthen collaborative leadership, strategic thinking, planning and decision-making skills. Communication development Members will develop their ability to communicate with different audiences, participate in structured dialogue and present policy recommendations. Improved understanding of EU–Kenya cooperation Participants will gain greater knowledge of the European Union’s partnership with Kenya, including policy priorities, program design, communication and civil-society engagement. Community impact Members will be able to connect national and international policy dialogue with the lived experiences and priorities of the communities they serve. Who Can Apply? Applicants must satisfy all the following requirements: Citizenship Applicants must be Kenyan citizens. Residency Applicants must reside in Kenya and be available to participate actively in meetings and related activities throughout the mandate. Age Applicants must be between 18 and 30 years old during the project implementation period, which ends in March 2028. A description of experience working with young people, including marginalised youth and young people in vulnerable circumstances. title: CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship 2026: 12-Week Online Fellowship for Aspiring Conflict and Security Analysts
summary: The CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship 2026 is a 12-week online professional development programme designed for emerging analysts who want to build practical expertise in conflict analysis, early warning, risk assessment, conflict data, OSINT, intelligence analysis, forecasting, and professional analytical writing , with a particular focus on African conflict and security contexts. The fellowship is designed to bridge the gap between academic knowledge and practical analytical skills. Participants will learn how to understand the causes and dynamics of conflict, assess evidence and information sources, analyze conflict data, identify early-warning indicators, assess political and conflict risks, develop scenarios, and communicate analytical findings to professional and policy audiences. The CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship Cohort 2026 will run from September to December 2026 , beginning on 14 September 2026 . The programme is delivered entirely online and has no fellowship fee for selected fellows . Applications are currently open, with the application deadline set for 31 August 2026 at 21:59 West Africa Time (WAT) . CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship 2026 at a Glance Programme: CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship Cohort: 2026 Duration: 12 weeks Programme period: September–December 2026 Start date: 14 September 2026 Format: Online Fellowship fee: No fee for selected fellows Time commitment: Approximately 4–6 hours per week Application deadline: 31 August 2026 at 21:59 WAT Focus: Conflict analysis, African conflict contexts, early warning, risk assessment, OSINT, conflict data, intelligence analysis, forecasting, and analytical communication Target participants: Emerging analysts, researchers, practitioners, journalists, policy professionals, students, and others working on or seeking to work on African peace, conflict, and security issues What Is the CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship? The CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship is a professional development programme focused on developing the next generation of analysts working on peace, conflict, security, governance, and related issues. The programme brings together several areas of analytical practice that are highly relevant to understanding contemporary conflicts. These include: Conflict analysis Evidence evaluation Conflict data analysis Open-source intelligence (OSINT) Early warning Risk assessment Intelligence analysis Forecasting Scenario building Professional analytical writing Policy briefing Rather than concentrating solely on theoretical concepts, the fellowship is structured around the practical skills analysts need to assess complex situations and communicate their findings effectively. The programme also places a distinct emphasis on African analytical contexts , allowing participants to explore conflict dynamics, actors, drivers, risks, and possible futures in relation to African countries and regions. Why Conflict Analysis Skills Matter Contemporary conflicts are complex and can involve multiple interacting factors. Political developments, economic pressures, social tensions, historical grievances, armed groups, state institutions, external actors, resource competition, misinformation, displacement, and other factors can interact to increase or reduce conflict risks. For analysts, understanding these situations requires more than collecting information. An effective conflict analyst must be able to: Identify relevant information. Evaluate the reliability of different sources. Separate evidence from assumptions. Understand the interests and incentives of different actors. Identify structural and immediate drivers of conflict. Recognize indicators of increasing risk. Assess the likelihood and potential impact of different scenarios. Communicate findings clearly to decision-makers. The CRCA fellowship is structured to develop these capabilities progressively over 12 weeks. What Will Fellows Learn? The programme is organized around four major stages: UNDERSTAND → ANALYSE → ASSESS → COMMUNICATE Each stage builds on the previous one. Stage 1: UNDERSTAND — Weeks 1–4 The first four weeks establish the foundations of conflict analysis. Participants will explore the nature of conflict, African conflict landscapes, key actors, interests, incentives, drivers, triggers, and accelerants. Stage 2: ANALYSE — Weeks 5–8 The next four weeks focus on evidence and analytical methods. Participants will learn about source evaluation, conflict data, OSINT, structured analytical techniques, hypothesis testing, scenario logic, and intelligence analysis. Stage 3: ASSESS — Weeks 9–11 Participants will then move from analysis toward assessment. Topics include: Early warning Risk assessment Political and conflict risk Forecasting Scenario building Indicators Thresholds Triggers Stage 4: COMMUNICATE — Week 12 The final week focuses on turning analysis into professional outputs. Participants will learn about: Analytical writing Policy briefs BLUF writing Oral briefings Portfolio development Final assessment Detailed 12-Week Fellowship Curriculum The fellowship follows a structured weekly curriculum. Week 1: Foundations of Conflict Analysis The first week introduces the fundamental concepts of conflict analysis. Participants will explore: Key concepts in conflict analysis Conflict typologies The role of the analyst How analysts approach complex conflict environments This foundation helps participants understand what conflict analysis involves and how analytical work differs from simply reporting events. Week 2: African Conflict Landscapes The second week focuses on conflict environments across Africa. Participants will examine: Regional dynamics Historical factors Structural drivers Patterns that influence conflict environments The objective is to strengthen participants ability to situate individual conflicts within broader political, historical, social, and regional contexts. Week 3: Actors, Interests and Incentives Conflict involves multiple actors with different interests and motivations. This module examines: States Armed groups Communities External actors Interests Incentives Relationships between actors Understanding these factors is essential for assessing why actors behave in particular ways and how their decisions may influence conflict dynamics. Week 4: Drivers, Triggers and Accelerants Participants will learn to distinguish between different types of causes and factors that influence conflict. The module covers: Structural causes Proximate causes Immediate causes Triggers Accelerants This distinction can help analysts avoid overly simplistic explanations of complex conflicts. ANALYSE: Weeks 5–8 The second stage of the fellowship develops practical analytical capabilities. Week 5: Evidence and Source Evaluation Participants will learn how to assess the quality and reliability of information. Topics include: Source evaluation Verification Bias Confidence levels Evidence assessment These skills are important for analysts who need to make judgments based on information that may be incomplete, contradictory, biased, or unreliable. Week 6: Conflict Data and OSINT The programme then introduces conflict data and open-source intelligence methods. Participants will explore: Conflict event datasets Open-source information Geospatial methods OSINT approaches The goal is to help emerging analysts understand how publicly available information and structured datasets can contribute to conflict analysis. Week 7: Structured Analytical Techniques Participants will be introduced to structured approaches for improving analytical reasoning. Topics include: Hypothesis testing Analysis of competing hypotheses Scenario logic Structured analytical techniques These methods can help analysts challenge assumptions, evaluate alternative explanations, and reduce the risk of premature conclusions. Week 8: Intelligence Analysis Practice The eighth week focuses on practical intelligence analysis. Participants will explore: Analytical standards Intelligence tradecraft Analytical integrity Professional approaches to intelligence analysis The emphasis is on developing disciplined analytical practices rather than simply gathering more information. ASSESS: Weeks 9–11 The third stage focuses on turning information and analysis into assessments of future risks. Week 9: Early Warning Systems Early warning is an important component of conflict prevention and risk management. Participants will examine: Early-warning indicators Thresholds Monitoring frameworks Methods for tracking changes in risk The objective is to help participants identify signals that may indicate changes in conflict dynamics. Week 10: Conflict and Political Risk Assessment Participants will learn approaches to assessing conflict and political risks. The module covers: Risk models Likelihood Impact Risk assessment This can help analysts move beyond describing what is happening toward assessing what may happen and why it matters. Week 11: Forecasting and Scenario Building The eleventh week focuses on anticipating plausible future developments. Participants will explore: Plausible futures Scenario building Watch indicators Triggers Forecasting Scenario-based thinking can help decision-makers prepare for different possible outcomes rather than relying on a single prediction. COMMUNICATE: Week 12 The final week focuses on communicating analysis professionally. Participants will learn about: Analytical writing BLUF writing Policy briefs Oral briefings Analytical portfolios Portfolio review BLUF , or Bottom Line Up Front, is a professional communication approach that places the most important conclusion or finding at the beginning of an analytical product. The final module is particularly important because strong analysis has limited value if decision-makers cannot understand the findings, implications, evidence, and recommendations. Who Is the Fellowship Designed For? The fellowship is intended for emerging analysts working on, or seeking to work on, African peace, conflict, and security issues . The programme is suitable for people at different stages of their early professional or academic careers. Potential applicants include: Early-career researchers Conflict analysts Security analysts Policy professionals Journalists Researchers Civil society practitioners Humanitarian professionals Governance practitioners Early-warning practitioners Peace and conflict professionals Postgraduate students Final-year university students Professionals seeking to develop analytical skills related to African conflict and security Applicants do not need to already be established intelligence or risk-analysis professionals. The fellowship specifically emphasizes that prior formal training in intelligence or risk analysis is not required . Instead, motivation, analytical curiosity, and commitment are considered important. Academic Backgrounds That May Be Relevant The fellowship is particularly relevant to students and professionals with backgrounds in fields such as: Peace and conflict studies International relations Political science Security studies Development studies Law Economics Related social sciences and policy disciplines However, the programme is not restricted solely to people with one particular academic degree. Professionals working in civil society, humanitarian action, governance, journalism, research, and early warning may also find the programme relevant if their work involves African peace, conflict, or security issues. Geographic Focus and Who Can Apply The fellowship has a clear focus on African conflict contexts . It is designed particularly for: African nationals African residents Individuals working substantively on African conflict contexts The opportunity is therefore strongly oriented toward people whose academic, professional, research, or practical interests are connected to conflicts and security issues in Africa. The programme description does not specify a single nationality or country restriction. Instead, it explicitly includes African nationals or residents and others who work substantively on African conflict contexts. What Will Fellows Receive? Selected fellows will receive access to a structured professional development programme and several learning resources. The fellowship provides: 1. A 12-Week Structured Fellowship Participants will follow a structured 12-week learning programme covering the full analytical cycle from understanding conflict to communicating professional assessments. 2. CRCA Emerging Conflict Analyst Field Manual Fellows will receive the CRCA Emerging Conflict Analyst Field Manual , designed to support their learning and analytical practice. 3. Fellow Workbook and Analytical Toolkit Participants will also receive a workbook and analytical toolkit to support the practical application of the concepts covered during the fellowship. 4. Weekly Analytical Seminars Weekly seminars will provide structured learning around the programme s core subjects. 5. Analyst Labs The programme includes Analyst Labs , which are practical, hands-on analytical sessions. These sessions are intended to move participants beyond theoretical learning and allow them to apply analytical methods to practical situations. 6. Mentoring and Portfolio Development Participants will receive mentoring and support related to building a professional analytical portfolio. This can be particularly useful for emerging professionals who want to demonstrate their analytical capabilities to future employers, research institutions, policy organizations, media organizations, civil society organizations, or other professional environments. 7. Practical Analysis of African Conflict Contexts The fellowship provides practical analytical experience using live African conflict contexts. This gives participants an opportunity to apply analytical approaches to real-world situations. 8. Professional Analytical Portfolio Participants will work toward developing a professional analytical portfolio. A portfolio can provide evidence of a participant s ability to conduct structured analysis and communicate findings. 9. Final Analytical Assessment Participants will complete a final analytical assessment as part of the programme. 10. Fellowship Certificate Fellows who successfully complete the programme will receive a CRCA fellowship certificate . Is There a Fellowship Fee? No. The fellowship is offered at no cost to selected fellows . This means selected participants do not have to pay a fellowship participation fee. However, applicants should carefully review any official programme communication for information about personal costs associated with internet access, equipment, or other participation requirements, as the provided information specifically states that there is no fellowship fee . Application Deadline The application deadline for the CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship Cohort 2026 is: 31 August 2026 at 21:59 West Africa Time (WAT). The online application form will close automatically once the deadline is reached. Applicants should therefore submit their applications before the final deadline rather than waiting until the last minute. How to Prepare a Strong Application Although the fellowship is designed for emerging analysts and does not require previous formal intelligence or risk-analysis training, applicants can strengthen their applications by clearly demonstrating their interest in analytical work. Demonstrate your interest in African conflict and security Explain the African conflict, peace, security, governance, humanitarian, or political issues that interest you. Highlight analytical experience Relevant experience may come from: Academic research Journalism Policy analysis Civil society work Humanitarian work Early-warning activities Research projects Conflict studies Governance programmes Select a strong writing sample Because analytical writing is a core part of the programme, applicants should carefully select a writing sample that demonstrates clear reasoning and evidence-based communication. Show curiosity and willingness to learn Applicants do not need to present themselves as experienced intelligence professionals. The programme specifically emphasizes emerging analysts, motivation, analytical curiosity, and commitment. Demonstrate availability The fellowship requires approximately 4–6 hours per week over 12 weeks. Applicants should make sure their schedule allows consistent participation. Why the CRCA Fellowship Could Be Valuable for Emerging Analysts The fellowship brings together several skills that are increasingly useful across research, policy, journalism, humanitarian action, governance, security, and international development. Instead of focusing on only one area, the programme connects: Conflict analysis + Evidence + Data + OSINT + Early Warning + Risk Assessment + Forecasting + Communication This integrated approach can help participants develop a more complete analytical workflow. For example, an emerging analyst may learn to move from: Identifying a conflict issue to Collecting and evaluating evidence to Analyzing actors and drivers to Identifying indicators and risks to Developing plausible scenarios to Communicating the findings in a professional analytical product. This progression is one of the central strengths of the fellowship. Potential Career Relevance The skills developed through the programme may be relevant to careers and professional activities in areas such as: Conflict analysis Peacebuilding International development Humanitarian affairs Security analysis Political risk Early warning Research Journalism Policy analysis Governance International relations Civil society Regional analysis Intelligence-related analytical work The fellowship does not guarantee employment or a particular career outcome, but the skills and portfolio developed during the programme can potentially strengthen an emerging professional s profile. Applications close on 31 August 2026 at 21:59 WAT . APPLY HERE What happens after the deadline? The application form closes automatically at the stated deadline. Applicants should therefore ensure their complete application is submitted before the closing time. Key Dates Event Date Applications Now open Application deadline 31 August 2026 Closing time 21:59 WAT Programme begins 14 September 2026 Programme duration 12 weeks Programme period September–December 2026 Conclusion The CRCA Emerging Conflict Analysts Fellowship Cohort 2026 offers an opportunity for emerging professionals, researchers, students, journalists, and practitioners to develop practical skills for understanding and analyzing conflict and conflict risk in African contexts. Over 12 weeks, participants will progress from the foundations of conflict analysis to more advanced areas including evidence evaluation, conflict data, OSINT, structured analytical techniques, intelligence analysis, early warning, risk assessment, forecasting, scenario building, and professional analytical writing . Selected fellows will receive the programme at no fellowship fee , along with a field manual, analytical toolkit, mentoring, practical analytical experience, portfolio development, a final analytical assessment, and a certificate upon successful completion. The fellowship is especially relevant to people at the beginning of their careers who want to build a foundation in conflict and security analysis but may not yet have formal intelligence or risk-analysis training. title: GEAF Ambassador Programme 2027: Join a Six-Month Global Climate Leadership Journey with Project Funding
summary: Applications are open for the GEAF Ambassador Programme 2027, a six-month international climate leadership initiative designed for people who want to turn environmental ideas into practical, community-based action. Organised by the Green Earth Action Foundation, the programme combines expert-led capacity building, personalised mentorship, project-management assistance, communications support, access to an international environmental network and funding for approved local environmental initiatives. Selected GEAF Ambassadors will develop and implement projects that address environmental challenges in their own communities. The programme’s central implementation milestone will be 4.29 Green Earth Action Day on 29 April 2027, when ambassadors in different locations will carry out coordinated community actions under a shared vision of local action and global impact. The programme is primarily conducted online. Participants must therefore be prepared to attend regular virtual sessions, work closely with the GEAF team, engage stakeholders in their communities and dedicate approximately five to ten hours every week throughout the six-month programme. GEAF Ambassador Programme 2027 at a Glance Programme name: GEAF Ambassador Programme 2027 Organiser: Green Earth Action Foundation Programme duration: Six months Delivery format: Primarily online, with projects implemented locally Expected commitment: Approximately 5–10 hours per week Main implementation date: 29 April 2027 Programme period: Early 2027 to summer 2027 Application status: Applications are currently open Application review: Rolling basis Official application deadline: No closing date has been published in the official programme page, Terms of Reference or application portal as of 18 August 2026 Funding: Support for approved local environmental projects, subject to programme rules and budget validation Application method: Online application through the official GEAF platform Information-session date: 26 August 2026 at 2:00 p.m. Zurich time Application email submissions: Not accepted About the Green Earth Action Foundation The Green Earth Action Foundation is an international, non-profit foundation headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. It was established in 2023 to support environmental protection, community-led climate action, sustainability awareness and inclusive environmental leadership. GEAF states that its work connects grassroots environmental mobilisation with broader advocacy, collaboration and systemic change. Its initiatives are aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and focus on turning environmental awareness into practical, measurable action. The foundation is listed by the United Nations Environment Programme as a UNEP-accredited non-governmental organisation from Switzerland. UNEP’s official register records the foundation’s accreditation date as September 2025. Accreditation provides eligible civil-society organisations with observer status and opportunities to participate in processes connected with the United Nations Environment Assembly. Applicants can independently verify this through the official UNEP list of accredited organisations . GEAF’s broader priorities include: Environmental protection Youth empowerment Community engagement Environmental awareness and advocacy Diversity and inclusion Peaceful coexistence between people and nature Practical community-based climate action The GEAF Ambassador Programme is the foundation’s flagship leadership initiative. According to the official programme page , its existing international network includes 40 ambassadors from 24 countries across five continents. What Is the GEAF Ambassador Programme 2027? The GEAF Ambassador Programme is designed to cultivate environmental leadership and mobilise sustainability advocates from different professional, academic, cultural and geographical backgrounds. During the programme, ambassadors are expected to identify an environmental challenge affecting their community and develop a realistic initiative that responds to that problem. GEAF then supports selected ambassadors through training, project planning, mentoring, communication tools and approved implementation funding. The programme covers the complete project lifecycle, including: Understanding the environmental challenge Designing a locally relevant solution Developing an implementation plan Identifying community stakeholders and potential partners Preparing a realistic budget Mobilising participants and volunteers Implementing the initiative Communicating the project to a wider audience Monitoring results and collecting evidence Completing reports and close-out requirements Remaining connected with the wider GEAF Ambassador Network Although 4.29 Green Earth Action Day is the programme’s major implementation milestone, the programme does not end immediately after 29 April. Ambassadors must continue participating in learning sessions, reporting and close-out activities before the programme’s formal graduation in summer 2027. Six Major Components of the Programme 1. Expert-Led Training and Development GEAF Ambassadors participate in structured learning sessions intended to strengthen their technical knowledge and practical leadership abilities. Training areas may include: International climate and environmental governance Sustainable development Climate communication Environmental advocacy Community mobilisation Partnership development Fundraising Innovation for sustainability Project sustainability Environmental justice Stakeholder engagement Previous GEAF training sessions have involved representatives or experts connected with organisations such as UNEP, UNDP, the International Labour Organization, the International Institute for Sustainable Development, the South African Institute of International Affairs, WIPO GREEN, the Climate Change Centre and other sustainability-focused institutions. However, applicants should understand that previous trainers and topics are presented only as examples. GEAF does not guarantee that the same speakers, organisations, subjects or training formats will be repeated in the 2027 programme. 2. Personalised Project Support Selected ambassadors receive one-to-one guidance from the GEAF team throughout the development and implementation of their projects. This support may cover: Defining the project’s objectives Developing an implementation plan Preparing and refining a budget Identifying potential partners Planning community engagement Structuring project communications Addressing implementation challenges Monitoring activities Preparing required reports Participants will also have continued access to the GEAF team for additional guidance, subject to the programme’s communication procedures and availability. 3. Structured Implementation Framework The programme establishes clear milestones, deadlines, reporting requirements and operational guidance across the six-month cycle. This framework is intended to help ambassadors move from a general environmental idea to an initiative that is specific, feasible and measurable. Ambassadors receive templates and guidance to support project organisation, implementation and reporting. 4. Communication and Visibility Support GEAF provides communication resources intended to strengthen the reach and visibility of ambassador-led projects. Support may include: Press-release templates Event invitation templates Social-media templates Guidance on media engagement Messaging and storytelling assistance On-demand design support for activity materials Promotion through GEAF’s communication platforms Ambassadors are expected to participate in relevant GEAF communication activities and provide accurate project information, photographs, results and supporting evidence when requested. 5. Grants for Local Project Implementation GEAF provides implementation support for ambassador-led environmental projects. The programme support framework states that each GEAF Ambassador receives a grant to implement a local project for 4.29 Green Earth Action Day. The programme’s Frequently Asked Questions further clarifies that funding for selected projects is subject to: Approval of the proposed local initiative Programme rules Budget review and validation Compliance with financial-documentation requirements Timely reporting Proper use of approved project resources The official materials do not specify a fixed grant amount. Applicants should therefore prepare a realistic and well-justified project budget without assuming a particular level of funding. The funding is intended for approved project implementation. It should not be interpreted as a personal cash award, salary or unrestricted allowance. 6. International Networking and Peer Learning Selected participants gain access to GEAF’s international network of current and former ambassadors, environmental professionals, experts and collaborating organisations. Networking opportunities may include: Exchanges with former GEAF Ambassadors Peer-to-peer learning Direct engagement with ambassadors from other regions Collaborative activities Knowledge sharing Future partnership opportunities Continued engagement after the programme cycle The programme aims to build long-term environmental leadership rather than limiting participants’ involvement to a single project or event. Environmental Project Areas Supported by GEAF Applicants must propose a community-based initiative connected with one of the programme’s five environmental focus areas. 1. Climate-Smart Agriculture Advancement Projects under this area should promote agricultural practices that strengthen climate resilience, conserve natural resources and protect local livelihoods. Possible activities may include: Farmer education Regenerative agriculture Soil-health improvement Water-efficient farming Climate-resilient crops Sustainable food-production practices Community demonstrations Agricultural waste reduction Local food-security initiatives A strong project should connect environmental sustainability with practical benefits for farmers, households or local communities. 2. Environmental Education and Community Empowerment This focus area supports projects that increase environmental understanding, build community capacity and encourage sustainable behaviour. Potential initiatives may include: Environmental programmes in schools Youth climate-leadership activities Public workshops Community awareness campaigns Sustainability training Educational materials Climate-literacy events Community dialogues Behaviour-change campaigns Projects should move beyond general awareness by showing how education will lead to measurable action or improved environmental practices. 3. Forestry and Biodiversity Protection Projects in this area should protect, restore or sustainably manage natural ecosystems. Possible interventions include: Tree planting Reforestation Habitat restoration Biodiversity conservation Community-based forest management Protection of threatened species Native-plant restoration Public education on ecosystem protection Community stewardship initiatives Applicants should consider plant survival, long-term maintenance, local biodiversity and community ownership rather than focusing only on the number of trees planted. 4. Marine and Water Protection This theme supports initiatives that safeguard marine and freshwater resources and promote responsible water management. Projects may involve: Beach, river or lake clean-ups Water-conservation awareness Plastic-pollution reduction Freshwater protection Marine ecosystem education Community water stewardship Pollution monitoring Sustainable water-use campaigns Restoration of aquatic habitats Applications should clearly identify the targeted water challenge and explain how the proposed action will create continuing benefits after the event. 5. Waste Management and Pollution Prevention This focus area supports initiatives that reduce waste, prevent pollution and promote circular-economy practices. Examples may include: Recycling campaigns Upcycling activities Waste-segregation systems Community clean-ups Plastic-reduction initiatives Zero-waste programmes Composting Sustainable consumption campaigns Reuse and refill initiatives Community education on responsible waste management Projects should explain what will happen to collected waste and identify appropriate recycling, recovery or disposal partners where relevant. Official Participation Requirements Applicants must satisfy the programme’s core participation requirements: Be at least 18 years old when applying Demonstrate a strong understanding of and commitment to sustainability and environmental justice Possess strong written and spoken communication skills Demonstrate experience in community outreach and implementing local initiatives Be fluent in either English or French Possess at least a basic understanding of English, even when applying as a French-speaking participant Be available for the complete six-month programme Commit approximately 5–10 hours per week Be able to attend mandatory online sessions and meetings Have access to a reliable internet connection Be prepared to implement a local environmental initiative on 29 April 2027 Be willing to complete communication, monitoring and reporting responsibilities There is no upper age limit. Applicants may be employed, self-employed, studying or managing other commitments, provided they can meet the required weekly commitment. Applicants may apply independently. Formal representation of an organisation is not compulsory, although GEAF particularly encourages applicants representing non-governmental organisations working in environmental protection, climate action, sustainability, community development, youth engagement or related fields. No specific university degree or minimum academic qualification is listed. The selection process instead focuses on leadership potential, community experience, project relevance, motivation and the feasibility of the proposed initiative. What GEAF Looks for During Selection Applications will be evaluated against predefined selection criteria. Motivation and Commitment Applicants should demonstrate genuine dedication to environmental action and explain why the programme is relevant to their present work and future goals. Leadership Potential Candidates should show that they can organise activities, inspire others, mobilise participants and maintain productive relationships with community members and partners. Project Relevance The proposed initiative should respond to an identifiable environmental need in the applicant’s community. Innovation and Creativity GEAF looks for original and context-sensitive solutions. Innovation does not necessarily require advanced technology; it may involve a more effective, inclusive or sustainable method of addressing a familiar problem. Potential Impact Applicants should explain the environmental and social results their project could create and how those results may continue after the initial activity. Feasibility The proposed project must be realistic within the available time, expected resources and local operating environment.
